metaDescription: Six mandoline slicers compared on blade sharpness, thickness adjustment, hand guard design, stability, storage and cleaning, from handheld to full-size.
expertTake: The OXO Good Grips V-Blade mandoline is our top pick because an angled blade, a stable frame and a handguard that actually holds food make it the safest and most comfortable to use. The Benriner 4-blade is the value pick for thin, precise Japanese-style slicing. Skip the mandoline if you slice only an occasional onion, because a sharp knife and a steady hand are safer than an extra blade in a drawer.
introParagraphs: A mandoline slices vegetables to a uniform thickness far faster than a knife can. That consistency is what makes gratins, chips, slaws and pickles cook and look even.

It is also one of the kitchen tools most likely to cause a cut, so guard design and stability matter as much as sharpness. We evaluated six models from the candidate pool using spec sheets, listing details and patterns in owner feedback, and ranked them by safety, control and ease of cleaning.

products.name: OXO Good Grips V-Blade mandoline slicer with adjustable thickness
products.description:
The V-Blade slicer uses a blade set at a V angle, so the cutting edge meets the food at a slant instead of straight on. That makes slicing smoother, especially with soft items like tomatoes, and reduces tearing.

A dial sets the thickness, a handguard holds the food and non-slip feet keep the frame steady on the counter. Compared with the handheld OXO, it is a full-size unit that sits on a work surface, and next to the Benriner, it has a more forgiving guard and a built-in set of julienne blades. The frame folds flat for storage, but it is bulky.

In year three, the wear is the blade edge, which dulls slowly, and the guard prongs, which can bend. Rinse right away, since dried starch is hard to remove, and never reach past the guard. A cut-resistant glove is a good idea for the last slice of any vegetable. The folding legs lift the front of the frame, which gives sliced food a clear path to fall into a bowl underneath, and that matters when you are cutting several potatoes for a gratin and want to keep the work moving without stopping to scoop slices away.
products.bestFor: A home cook who slices often and wants the most comfortable and safest full-size model.
pros: Angled V blade cuts soft and firm foods with less tearing
Dial adjusts thickness without removing the blade
Handguard holds the food so fingers stay clear of the edge
Non-slip feet and legs keep the frame stable while slicing
cons: Full-size frame takes drawer or cupboard space
Julienne inserts add small parts to wash and store

products.name: Benriner mandoline slicer with 4 blades, Japanese stainless steel
products.description:
The Benriner is the slicer many professional kitchens use. A razor-sharp Japanese stainless steel blade slices very thin and cleanly, and a knob adjusts the thickness with fine control.

It is light and slim, so it is easy to store and handle, but the handguard is basic and the frame less stable than the OXO. It is best for people who like thin cucumber, daikon or onion slices and who are careful. Compared with the Benriner Jumbo, it is more compact, and next to the OXO V-Blade, it is sharper and lighter but less forgiving.

Care is straightforward: rinse right after use, dry the blade and store it with the guard on. The blade is the part you will eventually replace, and Benriner sells spares. A cut-resistant glove is a smart habit with a blade this sharp. Many cooks who own one keep it for the jobs where a knife is hard to do well, such as a pile of translucent onion rings or a bowl of radish slices for a salad, and use a knife for everything else, which is a sensible division of labor for a tool with so little forgiveness.
products.bestFor: A cook who wants very thin, precise slices and is comfortable with a sharp blade.
pros: Very sharp Japanese stainless blade slices thin and clean
Four included blades cover straight, julienne and fine cuts
Light, slim body is easy to store and wash
Fine thickness adjustment gives control over slice width
cons: Basic handguard needs careful use and a glove
Lightweight frame is less stable than larger models

products.name: Benriner Jumbo mandoline slicer, Japanese stainless steel blade
products.description:
The Jumbo is a wider version of the Benriner, made for big vegetables. A larger track fits half a cabbage, a large onion or a thick sweet potato, so you do not need to cut items down first.

The same sharp Japanese blade is used, and the thickness is adjustable. Compared with the 4-blade Benriner, it is bigger and handles large items more easily, but it takes more space and has fewer included blades. Next to the OXO V-Blade, it is lighter and sharper but with less safety hardware.

Because of the size, a stable work surface matters. Rinse and dry the blade after use, and store the slicer flat. Use the guard and wear a glove, since larger items can slip as you get to the end. Cut a flat face on a round vegetable first, so it sits steadily on the track instead of rolling, and press with even, moderate force at an unhurried pace, because rushing a large head of cabbage across a razor edge is how most accidents begin.
products.bestFor: Big slicing jobs such as cabbage for slaw or large onions.
pros: Wider track handles large vegetables without cutting them down first
Very sharp Japanese blade gives clean, thin slices
Light body makes it easy to move and clean
Adjustable thickness suits slaw, pickles and chips
cons: Larger body takes more storage space
Safety hardware is minimal, so a glove is strongly advised

products.name: Gramercy mandoline slicer with 12 slice settings, black edition
products.description:
The Gramercy offers 12 slice settings, from paper-thin to thick cut, on a dial. It targets people who want many thickness choices for chips, gratins and thick-cut fries.

The base grips the counter and a food holder protects your hand, so the design leans toward safety. Compared with the OXO V-Blade, it offers more settings but a less refined blade angle, and next to the Mueller, it has fewer blade types but a simpler build. The listing does not make strong claims about blade steel, so judge it as a general-purpose slicer.

Wash the blade by hand and dry it, and check that the dial clicks into place. If the dial slips between settings, the slices will vary, so replace or return it. Test the slicer with a firm potato on the first day, because that quickly shows whether the thickness stays where you set it, whether the base grips the counter and whether the guard holds a vegetable without letting it twist, all of which are hard to judge from a listing alone.
products.bestFor: A cook who wants many thickness settings on a simple full-size slicer.
pros: Twelve thickness settings cover paper-thin through thick-cut slices
Non-slip base keeps the slicer steady on the counter
Food holder keeps fingers away from the blade
Middle cost tier for a full-size model
cons: Blade quality is less documented than the Benriner or OXO
Dial can slip between settings if the mechanism wears

products.name: Mueller Pro-Series 12 blade mandoline slicer, chopper and spiralizer
products.description:
The Mueller is an all-in-one kitchen tool that slices, dices and spiralizes with a set of interchangeable blades and a container that catches the results. It aims to replace several gadgets with one.

For meal prep, that is useful, since you can dice onions straight into the container and spiralize zucchini without a second tool. Compared with the OXO V-Blade, it does more but with more parts to wash and store, and the blades are less specialized. Next to the Benriner, it is bulkier and the slicing blade is not as thin.

Keep track of the blade inserts, wash them carefully with a brush and let them dry. A drawer of loose blades is a hazard, so store them in the supplied case. Expect the all-in-one design to make some compromises, so use it where convenience matters more than precision. The catch container also fills quickly with wet slices, so empty it into a colander or bowl when it is half full, and let the blades dry fully in the case so they do not stain or rust between weekly prep sessions.
products.bestFor: Meal preppers who want a slicer, chopper and spiralizer in one set.
pros: Twelve blades cover slicing, dicing and spiralizing in one kit
Catch container saves cleanup and speeds up prep
Food holder helps keep fingers away from the blade
One tool replaces several single-purpose gadgets
cons: Many small blades to wash, store and keep track of
Each blade is less specialized than a dedicated slicer

buyingCriteria.explanation: A sharp blade cuts cleanly and needs less pressure, which is safer than forcing a dull one. Japanese stainless steel blades, as on the Benriner, give thin, clean slices. An angled V blade, as on the OXO, glides through soft food like tomatoes. A dull blade crushes food and slips, so check that replacements are sold.

The handguard holds food and keeps fingers away, but only if it is comfortable to use, and many people drop it when it grips poorly. The OXO V-Blade guard is designed to hold food through the stroke. Even so, pair any mandoline with a cut-resistant glove, and stop when the food gets too small to hold.

A dial or knob lets you change thickness without swapping blades, and the best ones click firmly into place. Look for a range that covers about 1 to 8 millimeters. A wobbly adjustment gives uneven slices and lets the blade shift during use.

A slicer that slides on the counter is dangerous. Non-slip feet, folding legs and a wide frame, as on the OXO V-Blade and Gramercy, keep it steady. Lightweight models like the Benriner rely on your control, so place a damp cloth under them.

Extra blades for julienne or waffle cuts add variety but add parts to store. A container catches slices, as on the Mueller, but it also makes the unit bulkier. Choose extras you will use rather than the longest list. Most home cooks end up using two or three thicknesses and a single julienne cut, so a slicer with a clean main blade and one good accessory usually serves better than a kit with a dozen inserts that spend their lives in a drawer.

Starch dries onto a blade quickly, so a rinse right after use is the best habit. A flat or foldable shape fits in a drawer, and a case keeps blades covered. Models with many small parts cost time at the sink.

specDecoder.meaning: A blade set at an angle in a V shape so food meets the edge gradually. It reduces tearing and the force needed.
specDecoder.watchFor: The OXO V-Blade uses it, while many cheaper slicers use a flat blade.

specDecoder.meaning: A hard, fine-grained stainless that holds a very sharp edge. It gives thin slices but can chip if abused.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Benriner models list it, and it demands careful handling.

specDecoder.meaning: The span of slice widths the dial or knob can set, usually in millimeters. A wider range increases flexibility.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Gramercy lists 12 settings, but the real useful range depends on the blade.

specDecoder.meaning: Add-on blades that cut matchsticks. They are fitted in place of or over the main blade.
specDecoder.watchFor: The OXO and Mueller include some, and they need careful storage.

specDecoder.meaning: A glove made of a material that resists slicing. It is a safety accessory, not part of the slicer.
specDecoder.watchFor: Most mandoline cuts happen at the last slice, so wear a glove for the whole session.

howWeEvaluated.title: Blade quality
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at blade material and shape. The Benriner and OXO V-Blade stand out. This is based on the spec sheet and patterns in owner feedback, not our own cutting.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety hardware
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared handguards, stable bases and legs. The OXO leads. Models with little hardware were marked down.

howWeEvaluated.title: Adjustment control
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked how thickness is adjusted. Dials and knobs that click firmly earned credit. A loose adjustment ranks lower.

howWeEvaluated.title: Versatility
howWeEvaluated.description: We credited extra blades and containers for meal prep. The Mueller and Gramercy lead. We noted the added parts and storage.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleaning and storage
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored slim, flat designs and blade covers. The Benriner stores easily. All-in-one kits need more care.

cards.label: Full-size frame
cards.text: The OXO V-Blade and Gramercy have legs, bases and guards. They are steadier and safer but take more space.

cards.label: Lightweight frame
cards.text: The Benriner models are slim, sharp and easy to store. They need more care and a glove.

howToChoose.note: Choose full-size if safety and steadiness matter, and lightweight if you value a thin slice and easy storage.

rows: Thickness options and a stable base

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A sharp blade, a handguard you will actually use, a stable base and a thickness dial that clicks. Wear a cut-resistant glove.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The OXO V-Blade has the best safety hardware, the Benriner has the sharpest blade and the Mueller has the most variety.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You slice often or have children in the house. The OXO V-Blade's stable frame and guard are worth it.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You slice occasionally and are careful. A Benriner does the job at a low cost.

maintenance.why: Starch and juice dry hard on the blade and are difficult to remove. A rinse prevents sticking and dulling.
A brush keeps fingers away from the blade. Never wipe the blade edge with a cloth or your hand.

maintenance.task: Dry and store with the guard
maintenance.why: Moisture dulls and rusts the edge. A guard or case protects both the blade and your hand in the drawer.
A loose dial gives uneven slices. Tighten or replace the part.

maintenance.interval: Every year or two with regular use
maintenance.why: A dull blade crushes food and slips. Replace it when slicing needs more pressure.

faq.a: They can be, since the blade is very sharp and the last slice is the riskiest. Use the guard and a cut-resistant glove, and stop slicing when the food gets short.
Yes. Even professionals use one or a glove. A handguard that grips poorly is a reason to choose a different model.

For chips, about 1 to 2 millimeters, for gratins 2 to 3 millimeters and for slaw and pickles it varies. Test on a spare slice before cutting a large batch. Thinner slices cook faster and crisp more, but they also break more easily on a thin blade setting, so firm vegetables such as potatoes and beets handle the thinnest settings far better than soft squash or ripe tomatoes, which do best at a slightly thicker setting.

Most mandoline blades are not designed for home sharpening. Replace the blade or the slicer when it dulls. The practical sign is that you start pressing harder to get through a firm vegetable, or that tomatoes tear instead of slicing, and at that point the extra force is a bigger safety risk than the cost of new parts, so do not keep using a worn blade out of habit.

A handheld slicer suits small jobs and storage, but a full-size model is steadier for large batches. Choose by how much you slice. A handheld unit rests over a bowl and is held in one hand, which makes it quick to grab for a single onion or a couple of cucumbers, but it gives you less leverage and less support under the food, so a long potato or a whole zucchini is easier on a frame with legs.

faq.q: Can I put it in the dishwasher?
faq.a: Some parts can, but hand washing protects the blade edge and the guard. Check the manual for each part.
